title: Book 7, Chapter 22 — Nineteenth Year of the War—Arrival of Demosthenes—Defeat of the Athenians at Epipolae—Folly and Obstinancy of Nicias
paragraphs: Meanwhile the Syracusans were preparing a second attack on both elements, and Demosthenes and Eurymedon arrived from Athens with reinforcements. These came to about seventy-three ships, counting the foreign ones, and nearly five thousand heavy infantry, Athenian and allied. There were also large numbers of darters, Hellenic and barbarian, of slingers and archers, and of everything else in proportion. For the moment the Syracusans and their allies were considerably dismayed. They saw no limit or end to their dangers: in spite of the fortification of Decelea, a new army had come that was almost equal to the first, and the power of Athens was proving so great in every quarter. The first Athenian armament, on the other hand, recovered some confidence in the midst of its misfortunes. Demosthenes saw how matters stood and felt that he must not drag on as Nicias had done. Nicias had wintered in Catana instead of attacking Syracuse at once, and so had let the terror of his first arrival fade into contempt. He had also given Gylippus time to arrive with a force from Peloponnese. The Syracusans would never have sent for that force if he had attacked immediately, because they thought they could match him by themselves. They would not have found out their inferiority until they were already surrounded, and even if they had then sent for help, it would no longer have been as useful to them. Demosthenes recalled this. He knew well that on the first day after his arrival he, like Nicias, was most formidable to the enemy, and he determined to lose no time in drawing the utmost profit from the consternation his army inspired at that moment. He saw that the Syracusan counterwall, which kept the Athenians from surrounding the city, was a single wall. Whoever became master of the way up to Epipolae, and then of the camp there, would find it easy to take, since no one would even wait for his attack. So he made haste to attempt the enterprise. He took this to be the shortest way of ending the war: either he would succeed and take Syracuse, or he would lead the armament home, instead of wasting the lives of the Athenians on the expedition and the resources of the country at large.

First, then, the Athenians went out and laid waste the lands of the Syracusans around the Anapus. They carried all before them, as at first, by land and by sea, for the Syracusans offered no opposition on either element except with their cavalry and darters from the Olympieum. Next Demosthenes resolved to try the counterwall first with engines. But the engines he brought up were burned by the enemy fighting from the wall, and the rest of his forces were repulsed after attacking at many different points. He therefore decided to delay no longer. He obtained the consent of Nicias and his fellow commanders and went on to carry out his plan of attacking Epipolae. By day it seemed impossible to approach and climb up without being seen. So he ordered provisions for five days, took all the masons and carpenters, and took arrows and everything else they would need for fortification work if they succeeded. After the first watch he set out for Epipolae with Eurymedon, Menander and the whole army, leaving Nicias behind in the lines. They came up by the hill of Euryelus (where the former army had climbed at first) without being seen by the enemy’s guards. They went up to the fort the Syracusans had there, took it, and put part of the garrison to the sword. Most of the garrison, however, escaped at once and gave the alarm to the camps. There were three of these on Epipolae, defended by outworks: one of the Syracusans, one of the other Siceliots, and one of the allies. The alarm also went to the six hundred Syracusans who formed the original garrison for this part of Epipolae. These advanced at once against the attackers, but they met Demosthenes and the Athenians and, after a sharp resistance, were routed by them. The victors pushed on immediately, eager to achieve the aims of the attack without letting their ardor cool. Meanwhile others, from the very beginning, were taking the Syracusan counterwall, which its garrison had abandoned, and pulling down the battlements. The Syracusans and the allies, with Gylippus and the troops under his command, came from the outworks to the rescue. But they went into action in some consternation, since they had never expected a night attack, which was a piece of audacity to them, and they were at first forced to retreat. The Athenians, flushed with victory, now advanced in less order. They wanted to get as quickly as possible through the whole enemy force that had not yet been engaged, without relaxing their attack or giving the enemy time to rally. In this state the Boeotians made the first stand against them, attacked them, routed them, and put them to flight.

The Athenians now fell into great disorder and perplexity, so that it was not easy to get from either side a detailed account of the affair. By day, certainly, the combatants have a clearer notion of events, though even then by no means of everything that happens, since no one knows much about anything that does not take place in his immediate neighborhood. But in a night engagement (and this was the only one between great armies during the war), how could anyone know anything for certain? There was a bright moon, but they saw each other only as men do by moonlight: they could make out the shape of a body, but could not tell for certain whether it was a friend or an enemy. Both sides had great numbers of heavy infantry moving about in a small space. Some of the Athenians were already defeated, while others were coming up, still unconquered, for their first attack. A large part of the rest of their forces had only just arrived or were still climbing, so that they did not know which way to march. Because of the rout that had taken place, everything in front was now in confusion, and the noise made it hard to distinguish anything. The victorious Syracusans and allies cheered each other on with loud cries (at night the only possible means of communication) and received all who came against them. The Athenians, meanwhile, were looking for one another and taking everyone in front of them for an enemy, even when they were some of their own friends, now in flight. They kept asking for the watchword, their only means of recognition. By all asking at once they not only caused great confusion among themselves, but also made the watchword known to the enemy. They did not find out the enemy’s watchword so easily, because the Syracusans were victorious and not scattered, and so were less easily mistaken for others. The result was that when the Athenians met an enemy party weaker than themselves, it escaped them because it knew their watchword, while if they themselves failed to answer, they were put to the sword. But what hurt them as much as anything, or indeed more, was the singing of the paean. It was nearly the same on both sides, and so it caused perplexity. The Argives, Corcyraeans and any other Dorian peoples in the army struck terror into the Athenians whenever they raised their paean, no less than the enemy did. So, once thrown into disorder, they ended by colliding with one another in many parts of the field, friend with friend and citizen with citizen. They not only terrified one another but came to blows, and could be parted only with difficulty. In the pursuit many died by throwing themselves down the cliffs, since the way down from Epipolae was narrow. Of those who got down safely into the plain, many escaped, especially those of the first armament, who knew the country better. But some of the newcomers lost their way and wandered over the land, and in the morning the Syracusan cavalry cut them off and killed them.

The next day the Syracusans set up two trophies, one on Epipolae where the ascent had been made, and the other where the Boeotians had first checked the Athenians. The Athenians took back their dead under truce. A great many of the Athenians and allies were killed, yet even more arms were taken than the number of the dead could account for. Some of those who had been forced to leap down from the cliffs without their shields escaped with their lives and did not perish like the rest.

After this the Syracusans recovered their old confidence at such an unexpected stroke of good fortune. They dispatched Sicanus with fifteen ships to Agrigentum, where there was a revolution, to win the city over to them if possible. Gylippus, for his part, went again by land into the rest of Sicily to bring up reinforcements, since after the result of the affair on Epipolae he now hoped to take the Athenian lines by storm.

Meanwhile the Athenian generals met to consider the disaster that had happened and the general weakness of the army. They saw that their enterprises were failing and that the soldiers were disgusted with staying. Disease was rife among them, because it was the sickly season of the year and because the place where they were encamped was marshy and unhealthy. Their affairs generally were thought desperate. Demosthenes was therefore of the opinion that they ought not to stay any longer. He had risked the attempt on Epipolae with this in mind, and now that it had failed, he voted for leaving without further loss of time, while the sea could still be crossed and their recent reinforcement might at all events give them the upper hand on that element. He also said that it would be more profitable for the state to make war on those who were building fortifications in Attica than on the Syracusans, whom it was no longer easy to subdue. Besides, it was wrong to squander large sums of money to no purpose by continuing the siege.

This was the opinion of Demosthenes. Nicias did not deny that their affairs were in a bad state, but he was unwilling to admit their weakness, or to have it reported to the enemy that the Athenians in full council were openly voting for retreat. For in that case they would be much less likely to carry it out when they wanted to without being discovered. Moreover, his own private information still gave him reason to hope that the enemy’s affairs would soon be in a worse state than the Athenians’ own, if they persevered in the siege. They would wear the Syracusans out by want of money, especially now that their present navy gave them a wider command of the sea. Besides this, there was a party in Syracuse that wished to betray the city to the Athenians and kept sending him messages telling him not to raise the siege. He knew this, and in fact he was waiting because he hesitated between the two courses and wished to see his way more clearly. So in his public speech on this occasion he refused to lead the army away. He said he was sure the Athenians would never approve of their returning without a vote of their own. The men who would vote on their conduct would not be eyewitnesses of the facts, as they themselves were, and would not judge from what they had seen. They would hear it from hostile critics and be guided simply by the slanders of the first clever speaker. Many of the soldiers on the spot, indeed most of them, were now loudly proclaiming the danger of their position, but when they reached Athens they would proclaim just as loudly the opposite. They would say that their generals had been bribed to betray them and return. For his own part, he knew the Athenian temper. Rather than perish under a dishonorable charge and an unjust sentence at the hands of the Athenians, he would take his chance and die, if die he must, a soldier’s death at the hand of the enemy. Besides, after all, the Syracusans were in a worse case than themselves. They were paying mercenaries, spending on fortified posts, and now for a full year maintaining a large navy. They were already in difficulty and would soon be at a standstill. They had already spent two thousand talents and incurred heavy debts besides. They could not lose even a small fraction of their present force by failing to pay it without ruin to their cause, since they depended more on mercenaries than on soldiers obliged to serve, as the Athenians’ own were. He therefore said that they ought to stay and carry on the siege, and not depart defeated in point of money, in which they were much superior.

Nicias spoke positively because he had exact information of the financial distress at Syracuse. He also relied on the strength of the Athenian party there, which kept sending him messages not to raise the siege. Besides, he had more confidence than before in his fleet and felt sure, at least, of its success. Demosthenes, however, would not hear for a moment of continuing the siege. He said that if they could not lead the army away without a decree from Athens, and were obliged to stay on, they ought to move to Thapsus or Catana. There their land forces would have a wide extent of country to overrun and could live by plundering the enemy, and so would do them damage. The fleet, meanwhile, would have the open sea to fight in, that is to say, a wide sea-room where their skill would be of use, and where they could retreat or advance without being confined or hemmed in whether they put out or put in, instead of the narrow space, which was all in the enemy’s favor. In any case he was altogether opposed to their staying where they were, and insisted on moving at once, as quickly and with as little delay as possible. Eurymedon agreed with this judgment. But Nicias still objected, and a certain diffidence and hesitation came over them, with a suspicion that Nicias might have some further information to make him so positive.
